missing_details: The requirement that the poset be finite
The notion of a partially ordered set and that it is not a total order
Specification that linear extensions are chosen uniformly at random
Clarification that the probability is inclusive between 1/3 and 2/3
Existence of a pair of distinct elements x and y
refined_question: Given any finite partially ordered set P=(X,≤) that is not totally ordered, does there always exist two distinct elements x,y∈X such that, when a linear extension of P is chosen uniformly at random from all extensions compatible with ≤, the probability that x precedes y lies between 1/3 and 2/3 inclusive?
equivalent_formulation: Equivalently, in any finite poset P that is not a chain, there exists a pair of elements x and y such that the fraction of all linear extensions of P placing x before y is between 1/3 and 2/3 inclusive.
justification: The canonical formulation of the conjecture requires specifying that the underlying set is finite, that the order is partial (not total), and that one considers uniform random linear extensions; the title alone omits these critical details. The refined question restores all such requirements verbatim from the authoritative source, while the alternative formulation is taken directly from the equivalent statement given in the same article.
